rewrites.blindSummary:
The region's documented contact point with trans-visitor risk is prison placement, which national law sets: under criminal-procedure code Article D248 a trans prisoner is held according to the sex on their identity documents, so trans women still marked male are placed in all-male facilities. An investigation published in January 2018 recorded exactly that near the region's principal city: a trans woman, shouted at and threatened by inmates during three days in a men's facility after a 2014 transfer, and — in the capital — another trans woman, held under notorious conditions after a 2016 protest trial; the national detention inspector-general calls transgender detainees the group that suffers most in custody.

The inspector-general's May 2021 opinion, covering every place of deprivation of liberty in the country and built from some forty referrals since 2010, finds serious violations persisting: isolation by reason of trans status, untrained staff, and a 2016 depathologisation law never translated into prison rules. It recommends that detainees choose the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation and trans-only wings, and requires continuity of hormone and medical care — recommendations whose non-implementation is itself part of the documented picture for visitors who are detained anywhere in the country, including here.
rewrites.blindTangential: The far-right municipal pattern documented here targets LGBTQ pride events and organisations broadly rather than gender expression specifically, but cancellations and hollowed-out permits directly reduce safe public space for gender-nonconforming visitors and residents in affected communities.
blindSourceSummaries: An investigation posted 12 January 2018: under Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code men and women must be held in separate establishments, but placement follows the legal gender on identity documents, so trans women still recorded as male are held in all-male facilities — the group that, per the national detention oversight official, suffers most in prison. Region-relevant case: a trans woman, transferred in 2014 to a correctional facility near the region's principal city, was met by inmates shouting abuse; a fellow inmate tried to attack her with a knife and she spent two days in solitary confinement; another trans woman was held under conditions described as worrying after her 2016 protest trial in the capital; near the end of 2016 the justice ministry counted a small number of transgender detainees across several facilities.

A national detention-oversight opinion of 25 May 2021 (covering every place of deprivation of liberty in the country; prepared from referrals received since 2010 concerning transgender detainees): assignment to establishments or wards (male or female) is based exclusively on civil status, so the vast majority of transgender people are held in institutions or wards that do not correspond to their gender identity, and search procedures for persons whose civil-status sex does not match their identity add constraints such as isolation. It recommends guaranteeing every transgender detainee the possibility of choosing the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation, requires continuity of medical and hormone care with free choice of doctor, urges research funding, and faults the administration for not translating a 2016 justice-modernisation law into prison rules.

rewrites.blindSummary:
No trans-specific statute, enforcement series or incident record survives in this region's sources; that absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence, not as evidence of local safety. The national framework documented in this record applies unchanged in every local administrative unit.

That framework is centred on custody. Under criminal-procedure code Article D248 a prisoner is placed by the sex on their identity documents, so trans women still legally marked male are held in all-male facilities; a January 2018 investigation records one such detainee spending three days in a men's facility amid inmate threats, and another held in notorious conditions after a 2016 protest trial in the capital. The national detention inspector-general's May 2021 opinion — covering every place of deprivation of liberty, built on some forty referrals since 2010 — finds serious violations persisting: isolation for trans status, untrained staff, and a 2016 depathologisation law never written into prison rules; it recommends that detainees choose the sex of search officers and ward, prohibits identity-based isolation, and requires continuity of medical care, and names transgender detainees as the group that suffers most in the country's custody.
rewrites.blindTangential: A local Pride event was cancelled — an anti-Pride hostility action affecting the whole local LGBTQIA+ community rather than gender expression specifically, but it removes the region's public visibility event and signals a hostile municipal climate that gender-nonconforming visitors would encounter in daily interactions.
blindSourceSummaries: A national-framework investigation published January 2018 on trans women in the country's prisons — the custody framework the record applies unchanged to this region: Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code places detainees by the sex on their identity documents, so trans women still legally marked male are held in all-male facilities; a trans woman from a foreign country whose passport listed her as female spent three days in a men's facility amid inmate threats (an inmate tried to attack her with a knife), and another detainee was held after a 2016 protest trial in the capital; at the end of 2016 the country had a small number of transgender detainees, and the damages obtained for one detainee's detention conditions were symbolic. No region-specific event appears; the article supports the record's claim that this national custody framework applies throughout the country.

An opinion of 25 May 2021 by the national detention inspector-general, covering every place of deprivation of liberty and relevant to this region because its visits included a prison and a central police station in the region, with findings concerning a small number of transgender women held in those facilities. Built on referrals received since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons, it documents serious persisting violations — isolation imposed for trans status, staff untrained on trans issues, and a 2016 depathologisation law never written into prison rules or healthcare guidance — and recommends financing research, policies against discrimination, and suitable procedures for searching and assigning persons whose civil-status sex does not match their presented identity.

rewrites.blindSummary: Region research direction: mixed — the country's largest LGBTQ+ community and its biggest police raids coexist, with police acting without legal basis. In early 2025 police arrested dozens of men at a hotel in the capital at a reported "gay sex party"; organisers risk pornography-law prosecution with penalties up to 15 years; an international human-rights organisation's local branch called the police's "discriminatory and senseless harassment of LGBTI people ... has no basis in law" and demanded release of those detained. The capital is one of a small set of provinces where an international NGO found discriminatory regional regulations — and simultaneously the place with the country's densest LGBTQ+ infrastructure, media presence and monitoring-group offices; an assessor should expect both to be true at once. National climate from this record's sources: an October 2025 presidential decree listed "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among the country's non-military national security threats alongside terrorism and drugs, amplifying self-censorship (editors killing LGBTQ+ stories for fear of government reprisal); police deny violence and extortions in the 2022 death-in-custody of a trans activist based abroad arrested on drug charges at an airport while family members allege he was beaten. Model-estimate residual (route 3, best-knowledge delta): sheer scale of the community limits enforcement reach.
rewrites.blindTangential: The October 2025 national security decree framing LGBTQ+ visibility as a threat shapes the local climate beyond what provincial rules do — journalists and platforms self-censor, reducing the public support infrastructure that gender-nonconforming visitors and residents could otherwise rely on.
blindSourceSummaries: An opinion analysis (Aug 2026): an October 2025 presidential decree named "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" a non-military national security threat alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction; journalists report a constant chilling effect (editors killing LGBTQ+ stories fearing government reprisal or religious backlash); civil-society and independent media space has contracted since 2024-25; documented amid student-led anti-government protests.

An encyclopedia article on LGBTQ rights in the country supplies the national framework the capital stands under and documents the capital's raid pattern in detail: police arrested over a hundred people over a 'gay sex party' in the capital in mid-2017, detained a similar number at a gym sauna in the capital in 2017, and arrested around fifty at a sauna in the capital in late 2017, with small numbers charged in each case, all pursued under the pornography law. More recently it records dozens of people detained at a hotel in the capital in early 2025, a small group detained at another hotel in the capital in mid-2025, and tens arrested at a private villa near the capital in mid-2025 — offences there can carry up to 15 years' imprisonment. In 2018 a municipal social agency declared transgender people 'socially dysfunctional' and detained trans women in city-run 'rehabilitation' centres unless they signed statements promising not to repeat their 'offence'. Transgender people may change legal gender only after surgery and a judge's approval, and there is no general anti-discrimination law, so police action in the capital operates on pornography and morality provisions rather than any LGBT-specific statute.

An international human-rights organisation's 24 June 2025 press release responds to the arrest of tens of people in a raid on a 'gay party' at a privately rented villa near the capital, and situates it inside the capital's raid series: dozens of people were detained for participating in 'a gay party' at a hotel in the capital in early 2025, and a small group were detained following a raid on a different hotel in the capital in mid-2025. The organisation's local deputy director called the villa raid 'a blatant violation of human rights and privacy' that 'exemplifies the hostile environment for LGBTI people in the country', and demanded the release of those arrested. The release notes that police made the arrests without naming detainees or conducting judicial proceedings, and that those detained risk up to 15 years' imprisonment under the country's broadly worded Pornography Law.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The capital sits at the centre of the country's 2026 reversal on trans rights: parliament passed an amendment bill removing the right to self-identification, restricting legal recognition to traditionally accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandating medical certification, and creating new offences of coercion and allurement punishable up to life imprisonment — a de facto reversal of the 2014 constitutional self-determination ruling, cleared by both houses and awaiting presidential assent. The bill triggered rallies in the capital in March 2026, and a panel appointed by the national top court urged its withdrawal amid privacy and dignity challenges.

The capital is also where the country's trans population is most institutionally visible: the most recent national census recorded hundreds of thousands of transgender persons, of whom tens of thousands held identity documents — the documentation gap and the protest politics both concentrate here.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2026 national amendment bill strips self-identification, adds anti-"coercion" offences and mandates medical certification — a national climate that raises the cost of being recognised as trans in public in this capital as elsewhere; under that regime, the capital's own profiling script (transgender read as disguise or illegal migrant) becomes a more acute outing and detention risk than the law alone would imply.
blindSourceSummaries: A national-framework news release, 26 March 2026 — core source for the record's claims: the 2026 national amendment bill on transgender persons' rights removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandates medical certification, and creates "coercing or alluring" offences that could criminalise support systems; the release calls it a major reversal of hard-won rights and urges the president not to sign it. The country's last census recorded hundreds of thousands of transgender persons but only tens of thousands hold the identity cards essential for social security — the national documentation gap the record concentrates in the capital. No capital-specific event in this source.

A national news outlet's article on the 2026 amendment bill: approved by both houses and now awaiting presidential assent; it removes the right to self-identify in a reversal of the 2014 national top-court ruling; the record's capital-protest-politics claim is evidenced here — an activist told a press conference in the capital the community sought recognition without invasion and rights without humiliation — and a national top-court-appointed advisory panel has asked the government to reconsider amid privacy-and-dignity challenges. The government argues the narrower definition will make welfare benefits, job reservations and healthcare support more targeted while strengthening protections against exploitation and trafficking.

rewrites.blindSummary: Region research direction: worse than national on public-festival access screening — religion-based identity verification doubles as an outing mechanism for gender-nonconforming visitors. After a religious organisation publicly urged the autumn dance festival's organisers not to allow people of other faiths and to check national identity cards for entry, a political row erupted; in a city of the region organisers imposed identity-card verification, security checks with "male and female" boundaries and a ritual bow before a religious image as entry conditions. An identity-checked, religion-screened entry gate at a public festival is precisely the mechanism by which a gender-nonconforming visitor is examined and outed by authorities who are not supposed to be involved — and it is happening in named cities, not nationwide. National backdrop from this record's sources: parliament passed a 2026 amendment bill removing the right to self-identify, limiting recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandating medical certification for gender-affirming procedures, and creating offences of coercion or allurement of a person to be transgender punishable with up to life in prison — prompting nationwide protests from trans communities, with a panel appointed by the national top court asking the government to withdraw it; the national census recorded hundreds of thousands of transgender persons but only tens of thousands hold the identity cards needed for social security.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2026 national amendment bill strips self-identification, adds anti-"coercion" offences and mandates medical certification — a national climate that raises the cost of being recognised as trans in public in this region as elsewhere, even though it is not region-specific; festival-gate identity screening (this region's own finding) becomes a more acute outing risk under a regime that narrows legal recognition.
blindSourceSummaries: A national-framework news release, 26 March 2026, on the 2026 national amendment bill on transgender persons' rights, which the record's national-backdrop paragraph relies on: the bill amends an earlier 2019 law, removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandates medical certification, and creates offences of "coercing or alluring" a person to be transgender that the release calls reminiscent of historic-era provisions criminalising transgender persons for appearing dressed as women; the country's last census recorded hundreds of thousands of transgender persons but only tens of thousands hold the identity cards essential for social security. No region-specific content in this source (the record's city entry-screening claim is not covered here); the article supports the record's claim that this national framework applies in every state/province including this one.

A national news outlet's article on the same 2026 amendment bill: approved by both houses and now needing presidential assent; it removes the right to self-identify, limiting recognition, in a reversal of the 2014 national top-court "third gender" self-determination ruling; critics warn it could exclude many transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people from welfare benefits, and a lawyer called the medical-certification requirement an attack on the privacy and dignity of the individual, while the government argues the narrower definition targets those facing extreme and oppressive discrimination and prevents exploitation and trafficking. No region-specific content (the record's city festival-screening claim is not covered by this source); the article supports the record's national-backdrop claims.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This state/province is where the country's religious-enforcement apparatus has been most visibly exercised against gender expression: in 2021 its religious department issued an arrest warrant for a prominent transgender businesswoman over her presentation and mobilised over a hundred religious-affairs officers in a manhunt that preceded her leaving the country, an episode documented in international analysis of government-backed discrimination against LGBT people in the country.

The national framework applies unchanged here: same-sex conduct is criminalised with sentences up to 20 years and whipping, there is no legal gender recognition, and the day-to-day exposure for gender-nonconforming visitors runs precisely through this state/province's religious-offence enforcement.
rewrites.blindTangential: Anti-Pride hostility at the state/province level — the January 2026 probe into a 'Pride' gathering and the official stance against LGBT promotion — targets queer visibility generally and spills over onto trans visitors in the state/province's tourism corridor.
blindSourceSummaries: A country profile of an international legal-rights organisation (last updated 16 December 2025) with both the national framework and this state/province's enforcement: penal-code provisions criminalise same-sex intimacy and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment with whipping (a law enforced in recent years; applicable to both men and women, and usable against trans people), and religious-law enactments criminalise cross-dressing and "males posing as females"; state/province-specific content — the national top court struck down provisions of this state/province's religious criminal-offences enactment of 1995 as exceeding subnational power (2021), the state/province's religious authorities issued an arrest warrant for a trans businesswoman who failed to appear in court and announced the deployment of over a hundred religious-affairs officers, and a state/province religious court sentenced a small number of men to several months' imprisonment with strokes of the cane; over a thousand people had attended state/province-run "rehabilitation programmes" as of mid-2021, under a crackdown on the LGBT community ongoing since the 2018 election.

An international human-rights organisation's report release (10 August 2022) documenting the country's government-backed discrimination, including the episode this record leads with: in 2021 a transgender woman and cosmetics entrepreneur failed to appear in court in this state/province to answer criminal charges for "insulting Islam" based on her attire; the state/province's religious department issued a warrant for her arrest and announced it had mobilised over a hundred religious-affairs officers to hunt her down, then sought her extradition from a neighbouring country — a deployment the organisations cite as showing how far authorities go to enforce rigid gender norms (she was permitted to remain under international protection and later settled abroad). National framework context: the national penal code punishes same-sex conduct with up to 20 years in prison, religious codes in the national capital area criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity, investigations covered this state/province and several other states/provinces, and state/province-run "rehabilitation" programmes were found to internalise discrimination and foment self-hatred.
